title: A Uniform for the Clock
premise: In 1913, Rosalind Joubert drives for the formidable suffragist Edith Marchmont, quietly reading every letter that passes through their hands. When the season's floods close the only bridge out of the river town of Marlow Bend, Rosalind is trapped inside a community hiding a deadly secret: the mill owner's private police have been covering up worker deaths, and the evidence sits in letters Edith has been smuggling for months. As a magistrate's inquiry arrives to write the official record, Rosalind must choose between protecting Edith's movement and exposing the truth through an underground printing press run by the very people she once only observed. The book ends with Rosalind testifying under her own name at last — the record corrected, Edith arrested but unbowed, and Rosalind finding a family among the printers who refuse to let history be written by its victors.
about_author: Xanthe Coldharbour is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing suffrage-era correspondence in regional collections. They write historical fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Letters I Wasn't Meant to Read
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Establishes the routine: driving Edith Marchmont between speaking engagements, steaming open envelopes, resealing them perfectly. We learn Rosalind reads everything out of habit, hunger, and self-protection. Emotional beat: quiet loneliness disguised as competence.

chapters.title: Marlow Bend, Last Stop Before Winter
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. They arrive in the mill town for what should be a three-day visit; Edith is to speak at a textile workers' meeting. First glimpses of the town's tension — blackened windows, men who watch from doorways. Beat: unease beneath hospitality.

chapters.title: The Bridge Goes Out
chapters.summary: Multiple POV, mostly Rosalind. Floodwaters take the span; the ferry is suspended until spring. Edish decides to stay — 'a captive audience is still an audience' — over Rosalind's objections. Beat: the trap closes gently, almost politely.

chapters.title: A Room Above the Print Shop
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Lodging arranged with the Harker family, who run a small job-printing shop. Rosalind notices type trays hidden behind wallpaper samples. Beat: curiosity kindling into suspicion.

chapters.title: What the Mill Pays For Silence
chapters.summary: Tomas Harker's POV. He explains, obliquely, why his brother stopped coming home two winters ago. The mill's 'accident ledger' never records names. Beat: grief worn as caution.

chapters.title: Edith's Correspondence
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Reading Edith's mail, Rosalind finds letters referencing 'the winter count' — numbers of dead workers — sent to a London contact. Edith knows more than she says. Beat: betrayal and intrigue braided together.

chapters.title: The Magistrate's Clerk
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. A clerk arrives ahead of the flood-cut-off, announcing an official inquiry into 'labor conditions' convening in spring — conveniently after memories fade. Beat: the clock starts ticking.

chapters.title: Constance Vane, Mill Owner's Daughter
chapters.summary: Constance's POV. She runs her father's office with cold efficiency but keeps her own set of books. She meets Rosalind at a charity event and recognizes a fellow reader of other people's papers. Beat: wary mutual recognition.

chapters.title: The Accident Ledger
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Edith asks Rosalind to copy documents she cannot be seen holding. Among them: a stolen page listing injuries dated before the 'accidents' they describe. Beat: dread hardening into purpose.

chapters.title: Night Typesetting
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The Harkers print a clandestine sheet called The Winter Count. Rosalind discovers them mid-run and, instead of reporting it, corrects a typo. Beat: found family begins — acceptance through work.

chapters.title: A Uniform for the Clock
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, title chapter. Tomas gives Rosalind a printer's apron: 'Everyone here wears the same uniform; the clock doesn't care who you were before.' Beat: belonging offered, hesitantly accepted.

chapters.title: The Constable Who Looks Away
chapters.summary: Constable Aldous Pike's POV. He suspects the Harkers but owes Tomas his life from a mill fire. His reports grow carefully vague. Beat: complicity as mercy, and its cost.

chapters.title: Letters to London
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Edith's network wants the evidence moved before the inquiry; the bridge is closed. Rosalind proposes printing it locally instead — scandalizing Edith, thrilling the Harkers. Beat: first open rebellion against duty.

chapters.title: Constance's Second Set of Books
chapters.summary: Constance's POV. She confronts her father's foreman about falsified safety reports and is threatened with her own ruin. She copies a key page, unsure yet whose side it serves. Beat: a rival becoming a wildcard.

chapters.title: The Widow's Testimony
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind takes statements from mill widows for the underground paper, learning to listen as well as read. One widow refuses to speak unless printed under her full name. Beat: courage is contagious.

chapters.title: A Raid That Missed
chapters.summary: Pike's POV. Ordered to search the print shop, Pike warns Tomas with a knock-code ten minutes early. The press hides in a coffin bound for the churchyard. Beat: the noose tightens; loyalty deepens.

chapters.title: Edith and the Movement's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. She weighs the town's lives against the national cause and calculates that martyrs serve better than witnesses. Rosalind overhears. Beat: the mentor's fallibility revealed.

chapters.title: What Rosalind Read
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Confession scene: Rosalind admits to Tomas she has read every letter for years, including ones that could have warned the Harkers. Forgiveness is not instant. Beat: shame met with grudging grace.

chapters.title: The Foreman's Grudge
chapters.summary: Foreman Brack's POV. He identifies the widow who testified and burns the Harkers' paper stock in retaliation. Beat: villainy with a grievance — he was passed over, humiliated, dangerous.

chapters.title: Spring Thaw, Early Ferry
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The bridge repairs finish weeks early; the inquiry will arrive within days. Everything must be printed now or never. Beat: urgency compressing every relationship.

chapters.title: An Alliance of Inconvenience
chapters.summary: Constance's POV. Constance brings her copied ledgers to the print shop, offering testimony against her own father. Rosalind must decide whether to trust her. Beat: enemies choosing each other.

chapters.title: The Type Is Set
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The full edition of The Winter Count — testimonies, ledgers, names — locked in chase, ready for the press. Beat: held breath; the calm before publication.

chapters.title: Brack's Men at the Door
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Mill thugs storm the shop; the press is smashed, Tomas beaten, the forme stolen. Rosalind hides the widow's original statements in the flour bin. Beat: devastation and survival in one night.

chapters.title: Broken Hands Still Count
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Hospitalized, Tomas dictates the edition from memory to Rosalind, who learns typesetting by candlelight. Beat: inheritance of craft; love declared without words.

chapters.title: Edith Chooses Sides
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Seeing the smashed press, Edith abandons her arithmetic and pledges the movement's funds and lawyers to Marlow Bend. Beat: redemption of the mentor.

chapters.title: The Inquiry Opens
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The magistrate arrives; victors' historians begin their tidy record. Rosalind watches testimony get sanded down and realizes the paper alone won't be enough — someone must speak on the record. Beat: the moral crux arrives.

chapters.title: Pike's Report
chapters.summary: Pike's POV. Forced to file an official account, Pike instead submits the truth he has been softening for months, knowing it ends his career. Beat: justice outside the law, from inside it.

chapters.title: Constance on the Stand
chapters.summary: Constance's POV. She testifies against her father, presenting the second set of books. Her father's lawyer dismantles her character; she holds. Beat: duty inverted — loyalty to truth over blood.

chapters.title: The Stolen Forme
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind traces the stolen printing plate to Brack's office and retrieves it with Constance's help during the inquiry's recess. Nearly caught. Beat: caper tension; trust cemented.

chapters.title: Print It Anyway
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. With a borrowed press from a neighboring town, the Harkers reprint overnight. Rosalind sets the final line herself: every name, spelled correctly. Beat: triumph shadowed by fear of consequence.

chapters.title: The Town Reads
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The Winter Count circulates through pews, pubs, and the inquiry gallery itself. Widows stand when their names are read aloud. Beat: the town reclaiming its own story.

chapters.title: Arrest Warrants
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Warrants issue for Edith, Tomas, and the unnamed 'printer's assistant.' Rosalind can flee across the reopened bridge. Beat: the choice sharpened to a single point.

chapters.title: The Bridge Reopens
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Standing on the repaired span, Rosalind watches others cross to safety and turns back toward the courthouse. Beat: love against duty resolved — duty redefined as staying.

chapters.title: Rosalind Joubert, On the Record
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind testifies under their own name, reading the widow's statements aloud, admitting to reading every letter — and explaining why the town needed someone who did. Beat: climax; identity claimed at last.

chapters.title: Verdicts
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The mill owner is indicted; Brack flees; Edith receives a sentence she calls 'excellent publicity'; Tomas's conviction is suspended by public outcry. Beat: imperfect justice, real justice.

chapters.title: What the Historians Kept
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Years later framing device begins: Rosalind, older, donates the archive to a library, insisting the Harkers' names head the catalogue. Beat: reflection; the record held.

chapters.title: Letters Afterward
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Letters arrive from the widows, from Constance abroad, from Edith organizing from prison. Rosalind reads them openly now, answering each. Beat: warmth; correspondence as communion.

chapters.title: The Apron on the Wall
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The rebuilt shop prints its first lawful edition; Rosalind's old apron hangs by the door like a coat of arms. Beat: legacy made ordinary, which is the point.

chapters.title: A Family, By Choice and By Ink
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. A quiet supper above the shop — Harkers, released Edith, visiting Constance. No speeches. Beat: found family settled into daily life.

chapters.title: The Clock Keeps Honest Time
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, closing. Rosalind seals a letter — properly, openly addressed — and walks it to the post. Final line echoes the opening routine, transformed. Beat: peace earned; the story's circle closed.
